title: Ohio Becomes a Midterm Battleground Again
summary:
In recent presidential elections, Ohio has voted reliably Republican. But in this year's midterm elections, the state is once again a major battleground, where either party could win.

The Cook Political Report, a group that studies elections, rates both the race for Ohio governor and the race for a U.S. Senate seat as toss-ups. That means each one is too close to call. Several races for the U.S. House are also competitive. Election Day is about two weeks away.

PBS NewsHour reporter Liz Landers visited Ohio to learn how national issues are shaping voters' choices. One big concern is affordability, or whether people can pay for everyday things.

In Youngstown, a city built on the steel industry, old factories still stand along the Mahoning River. Many jobs left decades ago. This summer, a local bakery closed after 120 years, and a nearby call center is also closing.

Ten years ago, Donald Trump won over many working-class Ohio voters by promising to bring jobs back. Now Republicans are in charge in Washington and in Ohio's capital, Columbus. Chris Anderson, who leads the local Democratic Party, said Republicans promised to tackle inflation but have not made people's lives better.

In the Senate race, Democrat Sherrod Brown is trying to win back a seat. He won three Senate races in Ohio before losing two years ago. He argues that Republicans made life more expensive. His opponent, Jon Husted, has said in an ad that 32 years in Washington is enough for Brown.

Gas prices have risen because of the war with Iran. Last month, Husted broke with President Trump and said the war needs to end so prices can come down. At a recent Trump rally, some supporters said they are willing to wait.
why_it_matters: Close races in states like Ohio could decide which party controls the U.S. Senate, which shapes the laws that affect families across the country.

background_read: Midterm elections happen partway through a president's term, when voters choose members of Congress and many state leaders such as governors.
The U.S. Senate helps make the nation's laws, so a few close Senate races can decide which party controls it.
Some states usually lean toward one party, while battleground states are close enough that candidates spend a lot of time and money trying to win them.
Voters often judge the party in power by how everyday life feels, including the cost of food, gas and housing.
